The current target range of 3.75–4.00% (midpoint 3.875%) sits very close to both actual inflation and conventional estimates of neutral, and recent data argue for maintaining this stance rather than moving further. Headline CPI, after falling back toward 2.5–3.0% in late 2024 and early 2025, has re-accelerated in 2026, running at 3.40% in August and having printed above 4% as recently as May; that keeps the real policy rate moderately positive but not aggressively restrictive (roughly 0.4–1.3 percentage points, depending on whether one looks at the latest or recent peak of inflation). At the same time, the unemployment rate has drift up from around 3.5–3.7% in 2023 to 4.2% in September 2026, modestly above pre-pandemic lows and signalling some cooling in the labour market but not a sharp deterioration. Real GDP growth and industrial production both point to a resilient but not booming economy: quarterly GDP growth in 2025–26 is positive but not overheated (mostly 0.5–1.0% q/q), and industrial production growth has moved from negative in 2023–24 to moderately positive (around 1–1.5% year-on-year in 2026), suggesting activity has firmed but is not surging. Against this backdrop, the FOMC’s recent behaviour is telling: after a long plateau at 5.25–5.50%, they cut sequentially by 50 bps in September 2024 and then several 25 bps steps through late 2024 and 2025 as inflation moved closer to target and growth cooled, then paused at 3.50–3.75% for most of 2026 until delivering a single 25 bps hike on 17 September 2026 back to 3.75–4.00%, coincident with the inflation re-acceleration above 3.5–4%. Historically in this dataset, the Committee tends to move in short sequences of same-signed 25 bps adjustments only when the macro picture is clearly shifting (e.g. multiple cuts in late 2024–25, multiple hikes in 2022–23); a lone 25 bps adjustment often marks a fine-tuning move followed by a pause to assess incoming data. Given that inflation is somewhat above the typical 2% objective but not surging, unemployment is slightly above recent lows but stable around 4.2%, and activity indicators show steady rather than rapid growth, the dual-mandate balance now supports holding the rate after September’s modest hike rather than quickly starting a new tightening cycle or reversing that move. A further 25 bps hike to 4.25% would risk pushing real rates distinctly higher even as unemployment edges up; a 25 bps cut back to 3.75% would be difficult to justify with inflation still clearly above 3%. The pattern of past decisions and the current positioning of inflation, unemployment, and growth relative to the existing range therefore make a no-change decision the most likely outcome, with a reasonably high but not overwhelming probability around 0.7, leaving the upper bound at 4.00%.
